query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Preheat the build substrate to an optimized temperature (around 300°C) during SLM to reduce thermal gradients, thereby improving dimensional precision and mechanical integrity in HEA components.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built HEA components fabricated by SLM at room temperature that suffer from high residual stresses, warping, and internal defects caused by rapid cooling and severe thermal gradients.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled preheating step by raising the build substrate temperature to approximately 300°C with precise temperature controls and in an inert gas environment to minimize oxidation.
generation.conditions: SLM processing under an inert atmosphere with consistent substrate preheating across parts, applicable to high-performance HEA systems such as CoCrFeNiMn and similar alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: Elevated substrate temperature reduces the thermal gradient during solidification, leading to more gradual cooling, uniform melt pool solidification, and reduced residual stresses.
generation.mechanism: By moderating the cooling rate through substrate preheating, the intervention reduces the likelihood of crack formation and warping; this controlled thermal profile promotes even grain growth without excessive coarsening, thereby preserving dimensional accuracy and mechanical cohesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components fabricated with substrate preheating are expected to exhibit reduced warpage, lower residual stress levels, diminished defect density, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher tensile strength and ductility) compared to parts built on unheated substrates.
generation.baseline: Standard SLM processing at room temperature, which typically results in pronounced thermal gradients leading to high residual stresses, warping, and defect formation.
generation.boundary: Excessively high preheating temperatures may result in oxidation or unwanted grain growth; the optimal temperature of around 300°C is based on balancing stress reduction with minimal microstructural coarsening, but variations in HEA composition or part geometry may require adjustments.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies support preheating for stress reduction, the quantitative improvements in defect reduction and mechanical properties specific to different HEA systems require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of identical HEA components using SLM: one with substrate preheating at 300°C under inert atmosphere and one without preheating. Compare the dimensional accuracy, residual stress, and mechanical performance of the components.
measurements: Residual stress measurements via X-ray diffraction
Dimensional accuracy analysis using high-resolution 3D scanning
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in residual stress reduction, dimensional precision, and mechanical performance compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study uniquely demonstrates the processability, hot-cracking susceptibility, and in situ mechanical response of CoCrFeNiCu-HEA fabricated by L-PBF, providing new insights into defect evolution and mechanical performance under these specific processing conditions. Future work will focus on targeted alloying (e.g., Al addition), pre-heating strategies, and optimized scanning to further reduce hot-cracking susceptibility and enhance mechanical performance. This study provides insights into the processability, defect evolution, and mechanical response of L-PBF CoCrFeNiCu-HEA, guiding the development of crack-resistant, additively manufactured HEAs.

It has been highlighted that even small changes in processing parameters have a significant effect on the physical properties and microstructure of the final parts [], and even give rise to major defects in the parts, e.g., unreasonable process parameters [], internal defects induced by incomplete laser scanning filling [], geometric defects and macroscopic deformations under residual stress generated by apparent thermal gradients in the manufacturing process [], severe notching or deformation of the support bar. The literature [] illustrates the causes of these defects and concludes that the mechanical and biological properties of the parts are seriously affected. It is also found in the literature [] that the fatigue life of SLMed parts under multi-axle load is significantly reduced due to stress concentration caused by internal defects compared to forgings and that defects also affect the manufacturability, dimensional accuracy and surface roughness of SLM lattice structure [].
